responses.response: Model first, then views, and go from broad to detailed: 1) make sure the project includes `projects/shared`; 2) define the C1 scope with actors and the main SaaS system; 3) add relevant external systems if they matter; 4) add the C1 relationships and their technology; 5) decompose the system into C2 containers and container relationships; 6) create the primary C1 context view; 7) create the primary C2 container view and any focused C2 drill-downs; 8) add C3 components only for containers that need internal structure explained; 9) add `Use Cases`, `Deployment`, and `Operations` views afterward as separate concerns. Optional here: external systems, focused C2 detail views, C3 views, and all `Use Cases` / `Deployment` / `Operations` work. The rule is to stop at the lowest level that answers the question clearly.

No. A detailed C3 is optional. Create it only when readers need to understand the API container’s internal building blocks and internal interactions. If the API is simple and the C2 view plus a good container description already explain its responsibility and dependencies, stop at C2. If you only need to spotlight that container and a few neighbors, use a focused C2 view; go to C3 only when internal components, boundaries, or non-trivial internal flows matter.

No. That mixes two problems: `webapp` and `api` are C2 containers, not C1 elements, and temporal arrows describe behavior, not static context. The static structure belongs in a C2 container view. The ordered user journey belongs in a `Use Cases` sequence/dynamic view, because that is where step-by-step interactions such as `user -> webapp -> api` should live while C1 stays a clean actor/system overview.

Order: 1) call `understand-project-structure` first to find the target project, its `likec4.config.json`, shared includes, and existing conventions; 2) inspect the current model and existing C1/C2 views; 3) define the exact audience and scope of the new C2 view; 4) if you need to confirm allowed shared kinds/tags, call `lookup-element-kinds`; 5) if required containers or external systems are missing, call `create-element`; 6) if required flows are missing, call `create-relationship`; 7) build the new view with `design-view`; 8) refine filters, layout, focus, and drill-down with `customize-view`; 9) improve weak descriptions with `write-rich-descriptions` if needed; 10) validate with `test-model` and use `troubleshoot-errors` if the model complains; 11) record important trade-offs with `document-decision` when the view captures an architectural choice. If shared specs look stale, insert `sync-with-template` before step 2.

It should rely on other skills. Once the C2 is solid, hand production infrastructure to `model-deployment-infrastructure` and the nominal user scenario to `create-sequence-view`. If the deployment gets structurally deep, `name-deployment-nodes` and `structure-deployment-tiers` are the follow-on specialists. The modeling skill should stay focused on the logical model and static C4 views, because deployment topology and ordered scenarios are separate concerns in this workspace.

Order, without skipping: 1) start with `understand-project-structure` to re-orient in the multi-project workspace and identify the right project/config; 2) run `sync-with-template` because shared specs changed; 3) confirm the updated shared kinds and tags, using `lookup-element-kinds` if needed; 4) reopen the target model and make sure the container that needs more detail still fits the updated conventions; 5) if elements or links are missing, use `create-element` and `create-relationship`; 6) extend the target container to component level; 7) create the C3 view with `design-view`; 8) narrow it into a sensitive, focused view with `customize-view`; 9) after the static model is settled, hand off the nominal scenario to `create-sequence-view`; 10) finish with `test-model`, `troubleshoot-errors`, and `document-decision` if the shared-spec changes forced a modeling choice.
